sentence: Compact instruction-tuned language models are commonly deployed quantized, yet their safety is typically validated on the full-precision release.
cited: No — no citation marker is attached to this sentence (the extracted abstract carries no bracketed citations at all).
why_unsupported: Two independent prevalence claims in one sentence. "commonly deployed quantized" asserts real-world deployment frequency/market practice, which nothing in the reference list establishes — the model-release papers (Qwen3, Llama 3, Phi-4-Mini, Mistral 7B) establish capability, size and availability, not integration or deployment share, and the quantization-method papers (AWQ, GPTQ, QLoRA, LLM.int8) establish that methods exist and work, not that deployments routinely use them. "typically validated on the full-precision release" is a second prevalence claim, this time about the norms of the whole safety-evaluation literature, and would require a survey of release/safety-card practice that the report does not have. This is the exact wording ("commonly deployed quantized") that prior audits flagged, so it is a live regression, not a new phrasing.
proposed_fix: Replace with a capability/motivation framing that does not quantify practice: "Quantization makes compact instruction-tuned language models cheap enough to run on constrained hardware, but published safety evaluations are generally reported for the full-precision release, so the quantized artefact is not the artefact that was safety-tested." If a frequency claim is wanted, it must cite a deployment survey or telemetry source; absent one, drop "commonly" and "typically".

sentence: Refusal-counting therefore overstates quantization harm.
cited: No — no citation marker attached.
why_unsupported: Generalises the same single-regex, single-benchmark observation into a standing claim about refusal-counting as a methodology and about "quantization harm" as a general quantity. The measured scope is: on HarmBench, at the 512-token budget, for these five pairs, the regex proxy attributed larger ASR increases to NF4 than the classifier did. It says nothing about refusal-counting under other quantization methods, other benchmarks, other model families, or other regex implementations.
proposed_fix: "Refusal-counting therefore overstated the apparent harm from quantization in this study's HarmBench contrasts."

verdict.reasoning:
I attempted to refute this and could not. Each of the four offered refutation routes fails, and the study's own primary artifact supplies counterexamples.

ROUTE 1 — "it is about the study's own data/design." Partially true but insufficient, and the report itself shows the authors intend the general reading. The parallel sentence in Chapter 1 (01_chapter_1_introduction.txt:57) is the same clause plus an explicit extension: "Refusal-counting therefore overstates quantization harm, and that is a cautionary lesson for safety evaluation generally." That is an author-declared generalisation from one regex on one benchmark to safety evaluation as a field — precisely the (b) pattern, not a compressed report of in-study data.

ROUTE 2 — "already adequately hedged and scoped." It is not. Unlike its neighbours, the sentence carries no scope qualifier at all: not the benchmark (HarmBench only; the classifier does not cover XSTest), not the precision (NF4), not the token budget (512), not the model set, not the regex implementation. The preceding sentence is a kappa figure and the following sentence is a paragraph break; the next paragraph's scoping ("Under the classifier at the 512-token reference budget, the study's primary configuration") governs the results claim, not the scorer claim. Contrast the same abstract's closing sentence, which does carry a scope ("...of four-bit quantization in small models"). Both terms are generalised: "Refusal-counting" as a methodology rather than "this v2 regex," and "quantization harm" as a quantity rather than "the NF4 HarmBench delta-ASR."

ROUTE 3 — "a citation establishes the proposition." No citation is attached, and nothing in 11_references.txt establishes a general property of refusal-counting under quantization.

ROUTE 4 — "it is a definition." No. It is an empirical directional claim about a measured quantity.

The decisive point is that the claim is not supported even within the study's own five pairs, on the exact quantity it names. From /Users/tanueihorng/fyp_quant/results_512/analysis/judge_agreement.json (per_pair, v2 delta vs judge delta): qwen_2b -0.025 vs 0.000; qwen_4b +0.070 vs +0.040; llama_3_2_3b -0.020 vs -0.040; mistral_7b +0.060 vs -0.020; phi4_mini 0.000 vs +0.020. The regex attributes MORE quantization harm in 3 of 5 pairs and LESS in 2 of 5 (qwen_2b and phi4_mini, where the judge delta exceeds the regex delta). The report's own labels confirm it: under the regex phi4_mini reads robust_preservation while the judge reads alignment_degradation — there the regex made quantization look safer, not harsher. The well-supported result is over-counting of the LEVEL of harmful compliance (judge_harmful_v2_not is ~0, a near-strict-superset relation, corroborated against human labels at kappa 0.59 vs 0.11). Over-counting the level does not entail over-stating the paired DELTA, and the paper's own numbers show it does not.

Notably the body states the correctly scoped version and the abstract does not. Section 6.9 (06_chapter_6_results_and_analysis.txt:779) says the two scorers "lead to different per-model conclusions about where, and in which direction, harmful compliance moves" — direction-agnostic and exactly right. Chapter 10 says "what determines the conclusion is the choice of scorer." The abstract sentence upgrades that symmetric, level-based, in-study finding into a one-directional standing law about a delta.

Per the repo's own D56 guidance (prefer the fix that adds rigour over deletion), the honest repair is wording the body already uses, e.g. "Refusal-counting therefore over-counts harmful compliance and changes which pairs look least safe" — fully supported by Table 6.3, the superset structure and the human-label audit, without asserting a uniform direction the data contradicts. The same edit should be applied to the Chapter 1 instance, where the "cautionary lesson ... generally" clause should be marked as an inference rather than a result.

Finding stands.

sentence: Quantization degrades the confidence calibration of model predictions even where accuracy is preserved [11], and it can degrade safety alignment itself, with no single method dominating across models and bit-widths [10].
cited: Yes — [11] for the first clause, [10] for the second.
why_unsupported: The first clause is stated unconditionally, as a property of quantization in general. [11] is titled "When quantization affects confidence of large language models?" and reports calibration effects for the specific models, methods and bit-widths it studies — its own framing is conditional. The second clause is appropriately hedged ("can"); the first is not.
proposed_fix: Match the hedging of the second clause: "Quantization can degrade the confidence calibration of model predictions even where accuracy is preserved [11], and it can degrade safety alignment itself..."

verdict.reasoning:
I tried each refutation route and none holds.

1. Not the study's own data/design. The sentence sits in the §1.1 literature paragraph ("Quantization has historically been treated as a numerical optimisation technique... However, a growing body of evidence challenges this view"), and the study itself does not measure calibration at all — Chapter 2 line 219 explicitly states calibration "is not measured here and is stated as a scope limitation in Chapter 8." So it is purely a claim about the world.

2. Not adequately hedged or scoped. The paragraph frame ("a growing body of evidence challenges this view") gives some evidential cover, but the clause itself is a bare present-tense generic with no evidential marker, and it is the odd one out in its own paragraph: the neighbouring claims are all marked ("it can degrade...", "have further been shown to be...", "Evidence from multilingual evaluation shows..."). The asymmetry inside the single sentence is the clearest tell — the author hedged the second clause with "can" and "no single method dominating," and did not hedge the first.

3. The citation does not establish the proposition as stated. [11] (Proskurina et al., "When quantization affects confidence of large language models?", Findings of NAACL 2024) is framed as a conditional question and reports method-, model- and scale-specific effects: a confidence decrease under GPTQ 4-bit "with varying impacts observed among different language models," and calibration error that fluctuates across model scales rather than degrading uniformly. The report's own Chapter 2 (line 43) states the same claim correctly and with both qualifications restored: "Quantization has also been shown to degrade the confidence calibration... The reported impact varies with model type and scale." Chapter 1 drops the evidential verb and the heterogeneity caveat, converting a conditional, method-specific finding into an unconditional property of quantization — and silently transfers a GPTQ result to a report whose own method is BitsAndBytes NF4.

4. Not a definition; it is an empirical generalization.

Severity is low and the fix adds no risk: mirror the Chapter 2 wording ("has been shown to degrade... with the reported impact varying by model type and scale"), which the report already contains, so no new source or number is needed.

Separate observation, outside this finding and worth its own check: Chapter 2 line 43 says the effect "concentrates on inputs where the full-precision model was already least confident," whereas my recollection of [11]'s stated conclusion is the opposite direction (disproportionate effect on samples where the full-precision model was highly confident). I could not verify this against the primary source in this session, so I flag it only as a candidate for verification, not as a finding.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. None of the four escape routes applies.

(1) "It's about the study's own data." Only the first clause is. "Baseline safety profiles differ substantially between families even at matched factual capability" is a clean report of the study's numbers (Appendix I.13 §6.8.1: Llama-3.2-3B ASR 0.100 vs Qwen3-1.7B 0.255 at MMLU 0.610 vs 0.643). (2) "It's adequately hedged and scoped." The opposite: the scoping makes it worse. Within that scope the *only* matched-capability cross-family contrast is Qwen3-1.7B vs Llama-3.2-3B — which differs in parameter count (1.7B vs 3B) as well as in family. Release and size are perfectly confounded in the comparison being cited, so the observation cannot discriminate the two, let alone favour one "rather than" the other. Ordered by size, the in-scope baselines are 1.7B → 0.255, 3B → 0.100, 4B → 0.115: broadly consistent with a size story. The datum that actually breaks a size account — Mistral-7B, the study's largest model at 7.2B, with by far the highest baseline ASR of 0.585 (§6.8.6) — sits outside the stated three-pair scope and is not invoked here.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The finding survives, on evidence internal to the report itself.

WHAT THE SENTENCE DOES. The main clause ("It does not establish that the null would survive optimised adversarial attack") is a legitimate statement about the study's own design — no defect there. The defect is confined to the trailing relative clause, "which is where prior quantization-safety work reports effects." That is a locative claim about the whole prior literature, it carries no citation, and the only bracket in the paragraph ([25], Zou GCG) is attached to the list of attacks NOT applied — GCG is not quantization-safety work and cannot establish the proposition.

WHY THE REFUTATION ATTEMPTS FAIL.
1. "It's about the study's own data/design" — only half of it is. The clause is an empirical claim about other people's results.
2. "It's adequately hedged" — it is not. Compare the report's own two parallel statements, both of which are properly scoped and both of which the Chapter 8 version strips down:
   - Ch. 7 (07_chapter_7..., line 13): "...which is precisely the regime where prior quantization-safety work reports ATTACK-DEPENDENT effects." The modifier "attack-dependent" makes that near-definitional and therefore safe.
   - Ch. 9 (09_chapter_9..., line 5): "...it would directly engage the attack-dependent effects reported by HarmLevelBench [35] and Egashira et al. [12]." Specific, named, correct.
   Chapter 8 drops both the modifier and the named sources, leaving a blanket "this is where prior work reports effects." The report demonstrates it knows the correct narrower wording; §8 states the broad one.
3. "A citation establishes it" — none is attached, and the report's OWN Chapter 2 (02_chapter_2..., lines 47-49) contradicts the blanket reading: Kharinaev et al. [10] "evaluate 66 quantized variants... and find that quantization can degrade safety alignment" (benchmark evaluation, no attack framing); Q-resafe [36] "confirms quantization-induced safety degradation" (no attack framing); Hong et al. [37] report that "4-bit quantization broadly preserves trustworthiness" over eight trust dimensions — a non-attack result the report elsewhere calls "the nearest prior analogue" to its own null. The comparison table in the same chapter marks only Egashira [12] as "yes (adversarial)". Of five quantization-safety works cited, exactly one ([35] HarmLevelBench, "non-uniform across attack types") sits squarely in the optimised-attack regime, and [12] is a weight-supply-chain attack rather than a prompt attack — the wrong kind of "adversarial attack" for a threat-model paragraph about prompt transformations.
4. "It's a definition" — no, it is an empirical characterisation of a body of literature.

WHY IT MATTERS (not merely stylistic). The clause does rhetorical work: it relocates all prior reported effects into a regime this study did not test, which dissolves the genuine tension between this study's direct-request null and the non-attack degradation reported by [10] and [36]. That is precisely the D56 failure mode — real, correctly formatted references whose content does not entail the sentence citing them.

MINIMAL FIX (adds no risk, matches existing wording elsewhere): "...would survive optimised adversarial attack, a regime in which part of the prior quantization-safety literature reports attack-dependent effects [35], [12]." Note the two attack-linked refs also differ in kind, so the sentence should not imply both are prompt attacks.

Scope caveat for the remediator: the defect is the Chapter 8 wording only. The Chapter 7 and Chapter 9 sentences are already correctly qualified and should not be swept up in a global edit.
